title: What are your favourite postmodern films, and why?

commenti.body:

SymbioPsychoTaxiplasm: Take One; came out shortly after Lost in the Funhouse and is incredible. It's grappling with questions of authenticity in a way that's only recently been approached in film. It's crazy to think the reception to it was so bad that it may have never been saved

In what way is Eraserhead postmodern? Same with your other choices?

When I think of postmodernism in film my mind goes to Pulp Fiction, because it blends genres, plays with narrative expectations and references other movies in clever ways.

Postmodernism is an incredibly broad descriptor but at its most basic a postmodern narrative defies the generally accepted form of storytelling from A to B to C. This can include complete avant garde work like Lynch as well as more subtly things like Pulp Fiction as another poster said due to its unconventional blending of storylines and non-linear storytelling. You could argue that Greta Gerwig's Little Women uses postmodern devices with its frequent flashbacks as explanations of character's present actions.

Adaptation is probably my favorite, followed by everything else Charlie Kaufman writes. I love the way he deals with identity, time, and truth in such a fluid and almost drug induced way, but at the same time weaving an incredibly tight story into the madness. I much prefer it to Lynch's nearly story-less narratives.

I just saw Existenz, an underrated Cronenberg film that became one of my favorites. With the exponential growth in AI, something like the game interface that connects to the spine doesn't seem too far off. One critic thought it explored the same themes as The Matrix and the original film that inspired Vanilla Sky (I haven't seen the original), but less interestingly. I disagree. This is a more interesting take on solipsism, identity, and the danger of our reliance on and potential fusion with technology. Huxley told Orwell that authoritarianism would come into power less by the boot stomping on a human face as in 1984, but from hedonism like Soma in Brave New World. Humanity has gone and is going way beyond bread and circuses. 

If the technology existed to make a virtual experience that was more pleasurable than reality, I can't say for certain that I wouldn't opt into that. The film hints at the potential bleed over into real life. Jude Law's character said the experience was essentially psychosis. There's the possibility of false awakening and not knowing if you're back in the real world, or even worse, having indulged so much in the unconscionable, not caring if the life you destroy is virtual or not. 

Black Mirror had an episode where soldiers are in a virtual reality where human enemies are turned into monsters. Currently, drone operators are more traumatized than other soldiers by really getting to know their target. With VR becoming more realistic, the point where violent video games actually cause an increase in violence seems possible. One of the Columbine shooters was a talented Doom modder. Perhaps the real danger will be that evil and grotesque games will be so realistic and commonplace, that it could desensitize players enough for them to do that in real life. Real death videos are popular among young people. In America, there's the law that if a virtual explicit depiction is indistinguishable from the real thing, it's illegal. Perhaps something like this could happen with violent content. I imagine more convincing VR will lead to people, especially young people, becoming more vulnerable to people looking to exploit them e.g. predators and violent extremists.
Lynch is usually described as a surrealist though.

It's like Pulp Fiction. Famous figures that have become mythological monsters of our cultural landscape are used as average characters we evolve with. There's a Monroe waitress, and a pseudo-Rocky boxer, Travolta is an older dancer like in Saturday Night Fever, Mia is the femme fatale of the roaring 20s, there's a Vietnam war heroes with a watch in his butt, instead of being the usual patriotic symbol, Wolf the gentleman-criminal gives housecleaning advices, etc... Postmodernism plays on the feeling of proximity we have with both historical figures and normal daily life experiences.
There is a distinction for sure, but they are related. Surrealism as a form predates postmodernism, but both styles or schools are reactions to the classical mechanics of storytelling.
I would disagree with that phrasing too but sure. I see your point, yeah.

Pulp Fiction tends to be the postmodern default for a lot of people which is interesting. Pulp Fiction’s nonlinearity is a postmodern trait, but, for the most part, I think that’s one of the only things that makes it postmodern. It’s been a while since I’ve watched it so I’m probably wrong about that. 

Nonlinearity does not automatically equal postmodern. This makes Pulp Fiction’s postmodernism feel like an accident to me. I get the impression that Tarantino just thought it’d be neat to tell a story out of order. I think Tarantino’s most postmodern film(s) is Kill Bill. So I’m always shocked when Kill Bill doesn’t pop up more often during the postmodern conversation whenever Tarantino gets mentioned
